extracted.intended_audience: graduate students and advanced undergraduates in analytic number theory and complex analysis
extracted.subtask_description: Textbook presentation of the analytic proof of the prime number theorem via the zeta function and the ψ and ψ1 functions; includes key identities, contour-integral representations, uniform-convergence criteria for double sums, and preparatory complex-analysis material on conformal maps. Geared to carrying out rigorous asymptotic estimates and contour deformations to extract main terms and error bounds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of Tchebychev's ψ-function
rubrics_metrics.description: ψ(x) = sum_{p^m ≤ x} log p. Equivalently ψ(x) = Σ_{n ≤ x} Λ(n), where Λ(n) = log p if n = p^m and 0 otherwise; also ψ(x) = Σ_{p ≤ x} [log x / log p] log p.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: All three formulations are equivalent and may be used interchangeably; the Λ(n)-formulation is convenient for Dirichlet-series manipulations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reduction: ψ(x) ∼ x implies π(x) ∼ x / log x (Proposition 2.1)
rubrics_metrics.description: If ψ(x) ∼ x as x → ∞, then π(x) ∼ x / log x as x → ∞.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use crude estimates relating ψ(x) and π(x) (e.g., ψ(x) ≤ π(x) log x) for the liminf bound, and a slicing argument with 0 < α < 1 to obtain the limsup bound; the converse is also true but left as an exercise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reduction: ψ1(x) asymptotics imply ψ(x) asymptotics (Proposition 2.2)
rubrics_metrics.description: If ψ1(x) := ∫_1^x ψ(u) du ∼ x^2 / 2 as x → ∞, then ψ(x) ∼ x and hence π(x) ∼ x / log x.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use monotonicity of ψ and the inequalities comparing averages over intervals (choose α < 1 < β) to bound ψ(x) by differences of ψ1 at scaled arguments and pass to limsup/liminf.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dirichlet-series identity linking ζ and Λ (equation (5))
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This identity is obtained by differentiating the Euler-product/log-ζ expansion and is the fundamental bridge between ζ(s) and prime-counting functions; used inside contour integrals to relate complex-analytic objects to arithmetic sums.

rubrics_metrics.name: Integral representation of ψ1 in terms of ζ (Proposition 2.3)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This Mellin-type contour integral identity is proved by inserting the Dirichlet series for -ζ'/ζ and applying Lemma 2.4 termwise; it is the starting point for a contour-deformation proof of the prime number theorem.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contour-evaluation lemma for a^s / (s(s+1)) (Lemma 2.4)
rubrics_metrics.description: For c > 0, the vertical integral (1 / 2π i) ∫_{c - i∞}^{c + i∞} a^s / (s(s+1)) ds equals 0 when 0 < a < 1 and equals 1 - 1/a when a ≥ 1 (so the integral discriminates whether a ≥ 1).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proved by choosing an appropriate closed contour (half-circle to left or right of the vertical line), applying the residue theorem (poles at s = 0 and s = -1) and showing the arc integral vanishes as its radius → ∞; used with a = x/n to pick out the contribution of terms with n ≤ x.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strategy for proving ψ1(x) ∼ x^2 / 2 by contour deformation
rubrics_metrics.description: Start from the integral formula for ψ1, deform the integration line from Re(s) = c > 1 to Re(s) = 1, account for the simple pole at s = 1 (whose residue yields x^2/2), and show the remaining integrals along the new contour are o(x^2).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Key steps: (i) ensure ζ(s) has no zeros on Re(s)=1 (so you can deform), (ii) choose a large truncation height T and a small δ so the box 1 − δ ≤ Re(s) ≤ 1, |t| ≤ T contains no zeros, (iii) decompose the contour into segments γ1..γ5, estimate each segment using bounds on ζ and its derivative, and choose T large and δ small so the total error is negligible compared to x^2/2.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nonvanishing of ζ on the line Re(s) = 1 (used in contour deformation)
rubrics_metrics.description: ζ(1 + it) ≠ 0 for all real t (so no zeros lie exactly on the critical boundary Re(s) = 1).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This fact is invoked to permit choosing a small δ so that the box 1 − δ ≤ σ ≤ 1, |t| ≤ T contains no zeros; it underpins taking residues at s = 1 and deforming contours without crossing zeros.

rubrics_metrics.name: Estimates for ζ and -ζ'/ζ near Re(s) = 1 (input estimates)
rubrics_metrics.description: One needs polynomial/logarithmic bounds for ζ(s) and for -ζ'(s)/ζ(s) on and near the line σ ≥ 1, |t| ≥ 1: e.g., | - ζ'(s)/ζ(s) | ≤ A |t|^η (and in refined steps bounds like O(|t|^{1/2}) are used).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such bounds (cited from Proposition 2.7 of Chap. 6 and Proposition 1.6) give decay of the integrand F(s) = x^{s+1} / (s(s+1)) · ( - ζ'(s)/ζ(s) ) on the far vertical pieces and allow the integrals on γ1 and γ5 to be made ≤ const · x^2 / 2 by taking T large; precise exponents determine integrability and the choice of T.

rubrics_metrics.name: Residue extraction at the simple pole s = 1
rubrics_metrics.description: Near s = 1, ζ(s) = 1/(s − 1) + H(s) with H regular, so -ζ'(s)/ζ(s) = 1/(s − 1) + h(s) and the integrand has a simple pole at s = 1 whose residue equals x^2/2.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Accounting precisely for this residue yields the main term of ψ1(x); the remaining integral (over the deformed contour avoiding the pole) must be shown small compared to x^2.

rubrics_metrics.name: Uniform-absolute-convergence criterion for interchanging double sums (condition (8))
rubrics_metrics.description: Given a double sequence {a_{k,ℓ}}, if for each k the sum over ℓ of |a_{k,ℓ}| converges and the sequence of row-sums bk := Σ_ℓ |a_{k,ℓ}| satisfies Σ_k bk < ∞, then the double series can be summed in any order and rearrangements do not change the sum.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consequences spelled out: (i) iterated sums converge and orders can be interchanged, (ii) partial-rectangle tails can be made uniformly small (Cauchy-type control), (iii) any bijective reindexing of N onto N×N yields the same total sum; this is the natural analogue of absolute convergence for double series and is used to justify termwise manipulations of Dirichlet-series expansions inside contour integrals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dirichlet-series manipulations and multiplicativity rules (Exercises)
rubrics_metrics.description: If two Dirichlet series Σ a_m m^{-s} and Σ b_k k^{-s} (bounded coefficients) converge absolutely for Re(s) > 1, then their product equals Σ_n c_n n^{-s} where c_n = Σ_{mk=n} a_m b_k; special cases yield ζ(s)^2 = Σ d(n) n^{-s} and ζ(s) ζ(s − a) = Σ σ_a(n) n^{-s}.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These convolution identities follow from formal multiplication and absolute convergence; they are used repeatedly to express products of zeta/L-series as Dirichlet series with arithmetic coefficients (divisor functions, σ_a, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Representation of 1/ζ(s) as Dirichlet series via Möbius function (Exercise)
rubrics_metrics.description: For Re(s) > 1, 1/ζ(s) = Σ_{n=1}^∞ μ(n) n^{-s}, where μ(n) is the Möbius function.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Derived from the Euler product for ζ(s); the identity μ * 1 = ε (Dirichlet convolution) underlies inversion and is useful for analytic multiplicative inverses in Dirichlet series.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition and basic criterion for conformal maps (start of Chapter 8)
rubrics_metrics.description: A conformal map (in this text) is a bijective holomorphic function f: U → V (i.e., a biholomorphism). If f is holomorphic and injective on U then f'(z) ≠ 0 for all z ∈ U and f^{-1} is holomorphic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the working definition used to guarantee angle preservation and invertibility; note some authors use the weaker condition f'(z) ≠ 0 as the definition of 'conformal', but here bijectivity is required for conformal equivalence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explicit fractional-linear map between upper half-plane and unit disc (Theorem 1.2)
rubrics_metrics.description: The map F(z) = (i − z) / (i + z) is a conformal bijection H → D with inverse G(w) = i (1 − w)/(1 + w); it maps the real line onto the unit circle (omitting −1) with explicit boundary parametrization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This standard Möbius transformation example illustrates boundary behavior: continuity on the real line except at the point corresponding to infinity, and the explicit mapping of boundary points (e.g., x = tan t maps to e^{i2t}); useful model when constructing other conformal maps by composition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of power maps and branches to map sectors and half-planes (examples)
rubrics_metrics.description: Maps z ↦ z^n map sectors {0 < arg z < π/n} conformally to the upper half-plane; more generally z ↦ z^α (with an appropriate branch of log) maps H to a sector {0 < arg w < απ}. Boundary behavior depends on the chosen branch.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When applying power maps, choose branches (cuts) carefully so the map is single-valued on the domain; compositions with translations/rotations give conformal maps to arbitrary sectors and control boundary images.
